summary: Records a format for operators to publish their own mapping from IP address prefixes to simple, coarse-grained location information. Interested parties can poll the feeds and combine them with other geolocation data.

plainLanguage.summary:
An Internet provider can publish a list saying roughly where each of its IP address ranges is used. Other companies fetch that list and use it to place their services closer to their users.

The list is deliberately coarse. It names a country, a region and a city, and it lets the provider leave out any detail it does not want to share.

subtitle: A plain text file where a network operator tells everyone roughly where its IP address ranges are used.

tldr.problem: Services place users by guessing where an IP address sits. When an operator moves a block of addresses, no central place announces it, so the guess goes stale and the service slows down for those users.
tldr.mechanism: The operator publishes one text file. Each line names an IP address prefix and, where it is willing to say, a country, a region, a city and a postal code. Consumers fetch the file and merge the entries with the location data they already hold.
tldr.outcome: The format carries only coarse location and the RFC is Informational, so it is not on the standards track. The authors say the format is already in use, and Section 7 says a more flexible format is planned.

facts.label: Feeds processed by Google

today: RFC 8805 is an Informational RFC, so it carries no standards-track status, and no later RFC has obsoleted or updated it. The authors describe the format as one that is already deployed. Section 7 says a more expressive format, possibly JSON (RFC 8259), is planned, but that no such specification or implementation existed when the RFC was written, and no extension to the present format is anticipated.

sections.title: Why Operators Publish Location Feeds
sections.content:
Internet services often guess the location of an IP address in order to pick a nearby server, infer a likely language, or add context to a search query. When an Internet service provider (ISP) moves a block of addresses to a new site, those guesses go stale and the affected users can get a worse service.

No central place announces such a move. This RFC records a format that lets the operator publish the answer instead. The operator, which may be an ISP, an enterprise or any organisation that cares where its prefixes sit, writes a file that maps IP address prefixes to simple location facts. Interested parties fetch that file and merge the entries with the location data they already hold.

The format was made for operators that move often. Regional operators wanted to publish a location change rather than wait for geolocation algorithms to learn it, and technical conferences publish the location of their meeting networks in advance of each event.
sections.plainLanguage: Services guess where an IP address is, so a provider that moves its addresses can make those guesses wrong. This RFC lets the provider publish the correct location in a file that others can fetch.

sections.title: The Feed Format and Its Five Fields
sections.content:
The feed is a UTF-8 text file. Lines end with a carriage return and line feed pair, blank lines are ignored, and everything from a number sign to the end of a line is a comment. Every other line is a comma-separated record with five fields:

ip_prefix,alpha2code,region,city,postal_code

Only the first field is required. The IP prefix is a single address or a prefix in Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) notation, such as 192.0.2.0/24 or 2001:db8::/32. The alpha2code is a two-letter country code from ISO 3166-1 alpha 2, and parsers should read it without regard to case. The region is an ISO 3166-2 subdivision code such as ID-RI. The city is free text that must not contain a comma. The postal code is also free text, but its use is deprecated: new feeds should leave it out, because it is specific enough to point at a single building.

An entry with every location field blank means the publisher wants no location at all for that prefix, for example because the space is reserved, not yet deployed, or being redeployed elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: The feed is a text file with one line per address range. Each line names the range and, if the publisher wants, a country, a region and a city. Any of those details can be left out.

sections.title: How Consumers Parse a Feed
sections.content:
A reader has strict rules. A line with no prefix, or with a prefix that does not parse, must be discarded. A prefix that appears twice is an error, and the repeated entries should be logged for review. Where several entries cover the same address, the longest matching prefix wins, because it is the most specific one.

Optional fields that do not parse should also be discarded and logged. A parser must ignore any field it does not expect, so that a future version of the format can add columns without breaking today's readers. The RFC states that no extensions to the format are in use or expected.

Appendix A of the RFC gives a short Python validator that a publisher can run over a feed before releasing it. It checks the syntax of each line and warns when a line does not have the five expected fields. It does not check that every prefix in the file is unique, so a complete validator has to do that as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Readers throw away lines they cannot understand, and they prefer the most specific prefix that matches an address. A short Python program in the RFC checks a feed before it is published.

sections.title: Verifying and Refreshing Feeds
sections.content:
A consumer may treat a published feed as a hint and prefer another source. The RFC still sets out what a careful consumer should do. It should protect the integrity of the feed, for example by fetching it over HTTP with TLS. It should check that the publisher really is authoritative for the addresses in the feed, and ignore entries for which it cannot. It should check accuracy as far as is practical, and set thresholds so that entries that disagree too much are flagged for review.

Because a publisher can change its data at any time and without warning, consumers should keep a local copy and refresh it. Without other timing information, the RFC recommends refreshing no less often than weekly, and no more often than is likely to trouble the publisher. A publisher served over HTTP or HTTPS can say when to come back using the standard Expires or Cache-Control headers, and consumers should refresh before that time passes.

Finding feeds is not specified. To date they have been shared informally as web addresses passed around in email threads, and the contents are checked by ad hoc means: personal knowledge of the parties, and comparing the prefixes in the feed with the prefixes announced in the Border Gateway Protocol by the autonomous systems the publisher is known to run. Earlier drafts mentioned the WHOIS service and DNS-based schemes, but the authors say support for those was never implemented, so the text was removed.
sections.plainLanguage: Fetch the feed over a secure connection, check that the publisher may speak for those addresses, and keep a fresh copy. The RFC suggests refreshing at least once a week. Feeds are still shared by hand, so buyers usually check the prefixes against public routing data.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Publishers are told to think hard about privacy before releasing anything. The RFC points to the security considerations in RFC 6772 for a fuller treatment, and warns that hiding a location by leaving out detail has limits.

Each location field is optional so that a publisher can publish only the level of detail it is comfortable with, and the level need not be the same on every line of the feed. The postal code field is the sharpest case, because it can locate a person inside a single building. Such values must not be published without the express consent of the people being located.

Operators are also encouraged to tell their users and customers that they publish this information, and what the consequences are for them.
sections.plainLanguage: A publisher decides how much detail to reveal and can leave out any field on any line. Postal codes are the most revealing, so they need the consent of the people they point at. Publishers should tell their users that the information is being shared.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that self-publishing location data opens no new attack route, because the location of an IP address is never truly secret to begin with. For publishers it can make life slightly easier for an attacker, since a feed shows which prefixes are full of customers and which are not in use.

For consumers the risk is that the feed arrives from a hostile source. The RFC requires proper input validation and other defences, which it ties back to the integrity guidance in Section 3. A consumer that skips the checks carries the same risk as one that has a plain geolocation mistake.

Verifying authority matters. If the publisher is not checked, one operator could publish claims about addresses held by another. At present only out-of-band checks exist, such as comparing the feed against public IP allocation data.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing your own address locations does not open a new way in, because nobody's address location is secret to begin with. The risk is on the reading side: a feed can arrive from someone hostile, so readers must check the data and confirm the publisher may speak for those addresses.
